hypotheses.text: Ectodermal features (sparse hair, dental anomalies, and nail dysplasia) in GTPBP2-related Jaberi-Elahi syndrome are progressive and age-dependent rather than congenital, precluding them from serving as mandatory discriminating criteria to differentiate affected infants under 12 months of age from infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy (PLAN) or pontocerebellar hypoplasias.
hypotheses.rationale: If ectodermal findings only emerge with age, neonates and young infants with Jaberi-Elahi syndrome who present with hypotonia, congenital microcephaly, and cerebellar abnormalities will lack overt ectodermal changes, directly contradicting the premise that ectodermal signs are required to distinguish them from phenocopies at initial presentation.

evidence.text: Carter et al. note that ectodermal findings and peripheral neuropathy are most prominent in older individuals, and presentation features such as brain iron accumulation and ectodermal findings appear to be age-related.

source.quote: Our findings suggest that some aspects of the clinical presentation appear to be age-related; brain iron accumulation may appear only after childhood, and the ectodermal findings and peripheral neuropathy are most prominent in older individuals.

evidence.text: A 4-month-old female infant with molecularly confirmed Jaberi-Elahi syndrome due to a homozygous frameshift variant in GTPBP2 (c.1165_1166del) showed severe microcephaly, hypotonia, and developmental delay, but explicitly lacked overt ectodermal abnormalities on physical exam.

hypotheses.text: Dental anomalies have an overall penetrance of 15% or lower in GTPBP2-related Jaberi-Elahi syndrome, making specific odontological dysplasia an insensitive clinical criterion for distinguishing it from other childhood neurodegenerative diseases.
hypotheses.rationale: While ectodermal involvement often encompasses teeth, hair, and nails, reports indicate that tooth development anomalies are present in only a minor fraction of GTPBP2 patients, meaning clinicians cannot rely on dental manifestations for differential diagnosis.

evidence.text: Across published cohorts, dental anomalies are reported in approximately 10% of cases, while broader hair and skin manifestations occur in roughly 60% to 80% of patients.

hypotheses.text: Sparse hair (alopecia/hypotrichosis) is the single most sensitive non-neurological hallmark of Jaberi-Elahi syndrome after early infancy, occurring in greater than 90% of individuals surviving past 1 year of age.
hypotheses.rationale: Establishing whether sparse hair alone achieves sufficient sensitivity past infancy will clarify whether it can function as a core post-infantile clinical distinguishing feature from PLA2G6/PLAN or pontocerebellar hypoplasias, where hair density is typically normal.

new_directions.question_text: What is the exact age of onset for sparse scalp hair, eyebrow/eyelash thinning, and dystrophic nails in longitudinal case descriptions of GTPBP2-deficient individuals?
new_directions.rationale: Determining the median and earliest documented age of ectodermal manifestations will define the exact diagnostic window during which Jaberi-Elahi syndrome cannot be separated from pure neurodegenerative phenocopies by physical examination.

new_directions.question_text: Do non-truncating missense variants (e.g., p.Leu430Pro) produce attenuated ectodermal phenotypes compared to biallelic null/frameshift variants in GTPBP2?
new_directions.rationale: Clarifying whether genotype correlates with the presence, severity, or complete absence of hair and dental abnormalities will refine clinical criteria according to variant class.
